t: Those Who Retire a Decade Before They Retire
q: Unfortunately for everyone around them, their engagement primarily consists of attendance, not contribution.
The signs are plain to see for those interested in catching this cancer early before it metastasizes.
They start to refrain from offering opinions or viewpoints, often sitting quietly through meetings as passive observers.
Good leaders don’t accept the early retiree’s new reality. They put them in charge of key initiatives and projects and hold them accountable to critical milestones.
As the popular poster says, “Growing old is mandatory but giving up is optional.
Leaders who leave them alone offer implicit permission to do so. So, who retired early?

t: Top-Down Decision Making Is Old School
q: Without input or involvement from others, decisions become mandates rather than smart choices for problems.
Wisdom, after all, is in short supply. Allowing the wisest leaders to make the call seems like a no-brainer — except for those who have to live with and execute the decision.
They point to substantial evidence that those on the ground, closest to the problem or issue, often have the best insight about how to approach the challenge.
The most senior leaders frame or state the problem and then turn it over to those most impacted by the issue.
They know that the quality of any decision is only as good as its execution. Top-down decisions are rarely executed with vigor and focus.
Reserving big decisions for those with big titles is a throwback to the autocratic organizations of the past.

t: Team Members Who Excel Most at Managing UP
q: Leaders who don’t know about the efforts a team member makes on their behalf can’t reward them for their good work.
When a team member goes too far in this self-promotion and makes it clear they stand ready to help the leader in any way they can, they are thought to be kissing up rather than managing up.
But it becomes a much bigger problem when those who excel at kissing up don’t actually get the job done or create the results they tout.
The disparaging commentary between teammates about this “brown noser” can undermine team morale and create a negative team atmosphere.
Over time, they fall prey to cynicism and despair. Getting ahead, it now seems, has little to do with producing great work but everything to do with managing and kissing up.
They don’t depend on what team members tell them or allow the charms of self-promotion to color their view. They distinguish between words and deeds.
Believing in their own abilities and moving boldly toward their goals is what successful people do.
The boost given by those who endorse your vision cannot be overestimated.
This pushback is essential for creating a stronger forward plan.
These doubters can knock you to your knees and zap the positive energy from your bones.
In other words, they stress-test the vision before committing to it.
Exploring the idea first with supporters and mentors is about validation, not acceptance.
The truth is, doubters are only good for one thing: reminding you never to be like that.

t: Underused Value Angle: Science Class is Beautiful
q: I think that in school we're way too quick to tell students "when they'll ever use this" (that's utility on the graphic above) and we're way too slow to paint a picture of how what we learn in school isn't just stuff to be used but is stuff that lets us experience pleasure and meaning and beauty.

Human infants are born with craniums made up of four plates that have not yet knit together into a solid dome so that their heads can compress to fit through the birth canal, so that the brain within can then expand.

Open enough to grow and closed enough to hold together is what a life must also be. We collage ourselves into being, finding the pieces of a worldview and people to love and reasons to live and then integrate them into a whole, a life consistent with its beliefs and desires, at least if we're lucky.
Learning things in science is not just valuable for future scientists. It's not just a thing that'll pay off for folks going into medicine or engineering.

Science is valuable for our students and worthy of their time because it enables them to experience beauty and meaning and purpose and delight that apart from science they'd not quite ever get to experience.
And the thing we teachers have to accept, of course, is that no one else is more responsible for helping our students to see this than we are.

t: A Huge (But Secret) Key To Classroom Management Success
q: As part of my personal coaching practice I speak to a lot of teachers.
Most teachers don’t really know what they want and expect from their students from minute to minute, which means the students have to figure it out for themselves.
You must visualize in your mind’s eye how you want your students to pull out their laptops, for example, or clean their instruments or transition to another subject.
Many teachers gloss over nearly everything in the false belief that students will get bored. The opposite is true. Specificity is good teaching.
Studies confirm that when you explain why—even if the why doesn’t make sense—your friends, family, and people around you are more likely to go along with your plans, ideas, and leadership decisions.

Knowing what they are to do from opening bell to dismissal gives students a sense of purpose. It shifts responsibility from you, and having to narrate them and correct them through every this and that, to them, where they can feel empowered.

t: What You Think v. What Students Think
q: Teaching is successful only as it causes people to think for themselves. What the teacher thinks matters little; what she makes the child think matters much.

Cognitive science has made clear for us that our minds remember only that which we think about. It's such an important idea that in his primer on cognitive science, Why Don't Students Like School?, Dr. Daniel Willingham dedicates a whole chapter to it.
Because, Willingham argues, they're far more likely to think about what they are watching on TV than they are to think about what you're saying.

In other words, a big part of my job as a teacher of ninth grade students is getting them thinking as often and as deeply and as meaningfully as I can about the things that we're reading and listening and speaking and writing about.
In short, what we think and how we think matters greatly. Your mind, colleague, is a big deal. You are an intellectual athlete.
Students remember what they think about, and the quality with which information is stored is the quality with which it can be retrieved.

t: How Do I Get a Seat at the Table
q: In the contemporary organization of inclusion and consensus, leaders are bombarded by team members who want to participate in the decision-making that affects both them and the team.
Good leaders know that only so many people can be included in major decisions.
The best leaders solve this dilemma by distinguishing between input and advocacy within the organization and team.
Advocacy, on the other hand, is about actively staking out a position and persuading others to yield to this view.
Not everyone who wants to participate in a decision can be accommodated in most organizations.
Input and advocacy are different animals. Good leaders design decision-making processes accordingly.
Leaders, by their nature, are in the business of helping others.
They may be suffering from what psychologists call the "Savior Complex" or "White Knight Syndrome.
A leader will know they have a problem when their intense need to save, fix, and help others becomes their purpose for being.
Fixing the problems others face validates how smart, resourceful, and wise they are.
By treating people like projects worthy of fixing, they create a helplessness on the part of others that undermines independence in execution and performance.
In the end, the persona of the White Knight must die. Who knew helping could be such a problem?

t: Teaching Students Why We Review Like We Do
q: In my experience, we teachers can be deleteriously presumptuous about the degree to which our students understand how best to learn.
When students don't know how to learn, it can often be quite harmful to the level of effort they put forth in class. And we can hardly blame them for this

Retrieval practice: testing yourself on knowledge - that is, literally requiring yourself to pull information from memory and use it - is the best way to both know that you know it and ensure that you know.
Interleaved practice: mixing practice up to include skills and knowledge acquired both recently and further in the past.
when you conduct activities like this in your classroom, take thirty seconds to explain to students why this kind of activity is worth their time. That's a critical piece.
just be mindful with memorization like this that the quality with which the information is stored is the quality with which it tends to get retrieved

t: When a Disgruntled Colleague Infects the Team
q: As it turns out, the adage “one bad apple can spoil the whole bunch” is true, especially when it comes to teams.
It only takes one loud voice away from the table to raise the doubts and suspicions of otherwise satisfied colleagues.
The most vocally hostile team members are almost always the weakest performers or those who feel unvalued for their unique insight and wisdom.
So, the disgruntled go underground, becoming much more dangerous in the process.
The best leaders deal harshly with those who go to the dark side.
They invite criticism from any quarter but refuse to tolerate incessant complaining.
Good leaders always remember that negativity is the mortal enemy of performance.

t: Why Are the Smartest People Such Poor Listeners
q: Human beings can analyze or empathize, but they can’t do both at the same time.
This fact is why highly analytical people are typically poor listeners.
The precision with which they listen, however, actually prevents them from understanding the feelings, identities, and emotions involved.
While accurately processing the arguments, they miss the trees for the forest.
Listening without judgment is incredibly difficult for highly analytical thinkers.
Emotions, identity issues, status, and pride usually play an oversized role in whatever created the problem to begin with.
It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to know we can never do both at exactly the same time.
Their constant evaluation of everything around them puts others on edge and makes them defensive.
They look for faults in team members like they are looking for buried treasure.
The critical eye and dismissive attitude they maintain are actually deflections.
They avoid becoming tyrants of criticism by spending more time on solving problems and less time blaming others for them.
Complaints about others and their performance do nothing to improve the situation.
Highly critical leaders reap what they sow: team members who spend more time staying out of target range than performing to the best of their abilities.

t: Whats Taking You So Long to Decide
q: If it were up to any given team member, leaders would just decide and move forward.
To those waiting for a decision, it appears that leaders often do everything in their power not to make one.
When a leader commits to a decision, all the other options disappear.
Good decision-makers don’t commit to a path until they have to. That’s what good leaders believe.
Quality decisions benefit from both urgency and optionality.
Leaders who remain steadfast in their commitment to keep their options open usually make better decisions.
Yet another reason why leadership is both thankless and hard.

t: 7 Academic Benefits Of Effective Classroom Management -management/
q: Classroom management has always taken a backseat. Now it’s sitting in the trunk.
Along with a teacher’s expert knowledge of content, classroom management has the greatest impact on academic progress.
In an exceptionally well-managed classroom, students are focused and working for hundreds of more hours than a typical classroom.
They can get lost in the intrinsic joy of learning when they’re free from phones, social media, behavior disruptions, disrespect, chaos, and trying to be cool.
A well-managed class has a maturity level that grows throughout a school year to two years greater than the typical class next door.
Test scores, reading levels, writing and math abilities, work habits . . . you name it. All indicators of academic growth will skyrocket because of the undeniable, unstoppable benefits listed above.

t: The Circle of Power: Something Good for the Last Five Minutes of Class
q: Instead, he strikes what I call the gentle urgency balance, which I think is key for signaling Credibility to students.
Urgent: on the one hand, school time is a sacred trust, and that trust isn't being honored when students mill around aimlessly for minutes on either end of a class period.
It seems like they are more distracted than they have been historically, more eager to pack up, more fixated on what's next on their schedules.
All right, students, that's a good closing spot for today. Do me a favor and pack up your belongings right now and let's form into a standing circle.
All right! In honor of Thanksgiving, I'd like to hear from ten different folks: one thing you're thankful for. Go.
The Circle of Power - a really fun way to mix things up during those final, finicky moments of class between now and the winter break.
